title: India must listen to Nepal’s grievances while lending a helping hand
content_html:
The state visit of Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah to Delhi, eight months after he was voted to power as leader of the ‘GenZ’ movement that ousted the previous government, was anticipated as a chance to reset the turbulent India-Nepal relationship. Bringing Mr. Shah to India for a state visit, his first, was particularly important, given the Modi government’s tense ties with his predecessor K.P. Sharma Oli’s government; Mr. Oli was not invited to Delhi more than a year into his term and travelled to Beijing instead. Initially, Mr. Shah had also given New Delhi some worrying moments, with comments about boundary disputes, and a refusal to confirm a meeting with Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri, which led to the cancellation of his visit in May. Subsequently, some of the realities of governance, particularly after the massive flash flood in August, have warmed Delhi-Kathmandu relations. Following talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Mr. Shah thanked India for its immediate and unstinting support in the flood relief and rescue operations. Mr. Modi’s praise for Mr. Shah indicated the forging of a personal rapport on which to build the road map for ties. India announced a Development Cooperation Package — a generous ₹15,000 crore (about $1.6 billion) — for reconstruction and long-term development in Nepal. Another announcement, to offer Nepal access to Indian ports in Gujarat and Odisha, will go a long way in helping land-locked Nepal, particularly given the bilateral bad blood over the 2015 trade blockade. The inauguration of bridges, roads, trains, energy and fuel lines, an Integrated Check post (ICP) and an agreement to set up an IIT (its third offshore campus) are all signs of concrete plans to improve relations, as outlined in the joint statement titled “Viksit Bharat and Samunnat Nepal: Re-imagining the Partnership”.

Despite some of the heated rhetoric over ties, both sides appeared to have decided to deal with areas of differences in a less public manner. Mr. Shah’s persistent comments on the boundary dispute, and long-pending request for overflight access for two debt-ridden airports, were not dealt with directly, but in a broad reference about resolving “all outstanding matters” through dialogue. While the joint statement also said they would review all bilateral treaties, New Delhi’s contention that the “Eminent Persons Group” (EPG) report that suggested important changes to the 1950 Friendship treaty, is now “not relevant”, will ruffle feathers in Kathmandu which has been keen to update the treaty. The government must remember that along with the grand gestures, it is important to keep a close eye on Nepal’s grievances as well. If disregarded, these can trip up the broader progress and conception of the bilateral relationship, as spelt out by both leaders.

title: Karnataka needs a coherent policy on urban mobility
content_html:
While Karnataka has spent years disputing motorcycle owners’ right to carry paying passengers, Bengaluru — with the dubious distinction of having one of the world’s highest travel times per unit distance — struggles with inadequate public transport capacity and lacklustre intermediate options. The Supreme Court ruling on November 20 to dismiss Karnataka’s appeal was thus straightforward, allowing motorcycles to be registered as transport vehicles. The State has often called bike taxis unsafe, yet has not improved the prospects of safer options. Earlier this year, the Centre for Science and Environment estimated the number of buses in urban centres nationwide to be 70% short of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs benchmark and that 400 cities with populations between a lakh and 10 lakh altogether lacked organised bus services. In March, the BMTC reported a fleet of around 7,000 buses in Bengaluru, versus the 13,000 by 2025 envisaged by the Comprehensive Mobility Plan. Expanding the number of Metro stations also creates more demand for travel to and from stations, but the operating costs of the public transport corporation expected to serve that demand are not covered by the resulting increase in rail ridership.

Overall, Karnataka has struggled to set up a consistent transport policy. An expert committee recommended against bike taxis in Bengaluru for first- and last-mile connectivity and in favour of better walking infrastructure and bicycle rentals in 2019, only for the State to launch the electric bike-taxi scheme in 2021, then rescind it in 2024 over safety concerns and drivers’ disputes. The market for short booked journeys is also dysfunctional. But while allowing bike taxis could temper autorickshaw fares, the State must investigate drivers’ operating costs, the difference between the paid and the received amounts, and prevent large platforms from exploiting the market. Finally, while the Union Road Transport Ministry has reported that 46.2% of all road deaths involved two-wheeler users, two-wheelers’ safety relative to autorickshaws and cabs, by the number and distance of journeys, is unclear. The State should require aggregators to report injuries and fatalities and investigate the consequences of drivers’ earnings being linked to the number of trips undertaken. The Union government’s 2025 Motor Vehicle Aggregator Guidelines already address passenger security, fares, and insurance while allowing States to authorise privately registered motorcycles through aggregators. Karnataka should exercise this additional power. A large national programme is required to address funding for public transport, which is necessary even when it is not immediately profitable.

title: Revisiting monthly frequency of PLFS
author: G.C.  Manna
content_html:
To meet the growing demand for employment-unemployment statistics at a more frequent interval, the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation introduced the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) with its first round conducted in 2017-18.

The PLFS was launched primarily with two objectives: one, to produce detailed annual estimates of important labour force parameters based on a longer reference period of one year and a shorter reference period of one week (popularly known as the Current Weekly Status (CWS) approach) preceding the date of survey for both rural and urban areas of States and UTs; and two, publishing quarterly estimates of three key labour force indicators — the Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR), the Worker Population Ratio (WPR), and the Unemployment Rate (UR) — as per the CWS for urban areas of 22 major States as well as all-India. These parameters have significantly strengthened India’s labour market database.

title: A changing Washington, a shift in U.S.-Israel ties
author: R. Swaminathan
content_html:
On the morning of the midterm elections in the United States on November 3, U.S. President Donald Trump announced that the U.S. would stop giving Israel about $4 billion a year, under a deal he said he had made with Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu months earlier. The announcement was widely seen as a last-minute attempt to limit the damage to the Republicans. It failed. But it was a tacit admission by Mr. Trump that unconditional support for Israel had become a political liability.

The Republicans suffered a heavy defeat, with the Democrats winning both the Senate and the House. U.S. Vice-President J.D. Vance went further, saying the Iran war was the reason that the Republicans had lost, and called on the party to change its relationship with Israel.

title: Letters to The Editor — November 25, 2026
content_html:
Beyond financial aid

India’s monetary aid to Nepal for restoring normalcy is welcome. However, the fragile glaciers of the Himalayas pose a serious threat to the people of Nepal, irrespective of climate conditions. When massive glaciers melt, it is not merely water that rushes downstream but a thick mixture of water, mud and rocks that can flatten even concrete buildings within minutes. The torrents surging through narrow valleys can alter the landscape itself. In such circumstances, humanitarian assistance for rehabilitation and reconstruction cannot, by itself, prevent future disasters. Given the fragile ecology of the Himalayas, a comprehensive master plan is needed to safeguard the people of Nepal, and India must work with Nepal towards this goal (Front page, “India offers ₹15,000 cr. in aid to flood-hit Nepal”, November 24).

V. Lakshmanan,

Tirupur, Tamil Nadu

Road safety and parents

title: Who pays for climate change is a federal question
author: Mukund P. Unny
content_html:
In the 1990s, several U.S. States sued the tobacco companies to hold them accountable for the health hazards of cigarettes. This litigation led to a 1998 Master Settlement Agreement, under which the companies committed at least $206 billion over 25 years as compensation for the harmful effects of cigarettes. Inspired by the famous tobacco litigation case of the 1990s, a small county called Boulder in Colorado, U.S., initiated a major litigation under the State law, in 2018, to fix liability on major oil and gas companies for the impact of climate change.

The suit claimed compensation for recovering the costs of coping with wildfires, floods and heat by building a case on public nuisance and consumer protection. In May 2025, the Colorado Supreme Court allowed the suit to proceed, holding that federal law did not pre-empt Boulder’s claims for damages under State law.

The oil companies, now backed by the Donald Trump administration, argue that federal law, including the Clean Air Act and the very structure of the American Constitution, forbids a State from applying its own law to global emissions.

They argue that a State cannot use its own tort law to make companies pay for harm from global emissions. This case has now ended up in the U.S. Supreme Court which recently heard arguments on the most important question in climate governance: who pays for climate disasters, and whether States have a role in formulating climate policy?

Since climate change is an international phenomenon, the issue in the U.S. has a direct nexus with India. When climate disasters affect India, its States are left to its own devices, with little help from any direction. When landslides tore through Mundakkai and Chooralmala in Wayanad on July 30, 2024, the Keralam government reported 298 deaths and 32 missing people. The Union took nearly five months to declare the tragedy a “disaster of severe nature”, and when assistance for rehabilitation came, it came not as a grant but as a 50-year interest-free loan of ₹529.50 crore. After the 2023 floods in Himachal Pradesh, the State government pegged the losses at ₹9,042 crore. Even though the Union Government released ₹633.73 crore in NDRF assistance for immediate relief, it sanctioned only a meagre ₹2,006.40 crore for recovery and reconstruction plan nearly two years after the disaster. In Punjab, after the floods of August and September 2025, the State government demanded ₹20,000 crore in immediate relief. The Union government announced only ₹1,600 crore as the relief. Like in Boulder, the governments that bear the costs of climate disasters are not the ones that control the climate policy.

title: Fatal disagreement: on the COP31 summit
content_html:
COP31 ended in Antalya, Türkiye, with a whimper. The 190-odd countries that had convened for nearly 12 days — a close to 50-hour overshoot — failed to agree on an overarching political statement, called a cover text, that acts as a stepping stone to future, collective global action on climate change. Usually, cover texts evolve as a final synthesis of deliberations; the COP31 leadership, helmed by Türkiye and Australia, thought it fit to push for a cover text early in the proceedings. The headline sought was a global electrification target: 35% of global final energy consumption will come from electricity by 2035, in the hope that this would reduce direct fossil fuel emissions. Ultimately, the cover text failed to pass muster because the European Union objected to the text’s lack of any explicit mention of ‘fossil fuel,’ let alone its phase-out. The COP process is arduously protracted as even a single country’s objection can stall progress. Country-blocks outside the EU, such as coalitions of the least developed countries, island nations, some South American countries — reportedly 130 countries — were also insistent on fossil fuel language. While COP 31 made some progress on old pathways, such as the Just Transition agreement, it is perplexing that the delegations could not make progress on the other big prong of negotiations: climate finance.

The increase in solar panel installations and the significant shift towards battery use in grid storage and transport did not come cheap: the cost of the land required for their installation, their intermittent nature of being dependent on weather, grid upgrades all carry costs. It is global markets, imperfectly connected, but connected, that have managed to bring it to this stage over decades. India and China, major fossil emitters, with large, still indigent populations, are also leaders in total clean energy installations. Therefore it stands to reason that developed countries, which have committed to providing climate finance in recognition of their historical emissions, make good on past promises to shoulder the cost of the carbon emissions that are responsible for warming. Economic crises are a feature, and not a bug, of the interconnected financial system enveloping the world and there are, undeniably, challenges to diverting the necessary finance towards countries most vulnerable to climate change impact. However, it is no longer prudent to sweep this under the rug by scuttling experimental approaches — namely carbon capture — as inimical to the broader commitment to eschew fossil fuel. When the primary framework climate agreement was crafted three decades ago, nobody envisaged AI and the drain that data centres portended or the wars that would see the vociferous antagonists of coal immediately shore up their gas reserves. Without honest good-faith dialogue, the COP is at risk of being a sideshow: a mortal blow to multilateralism.

title: Just verdict: on Myanmar and the International Court of Justice
content_html:
On November 19, the International Court of Justice held that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. It is for the first time that the court has found any state responsible for the crime. The verdict, with nine votes to six, was not lightly reached. Genocide requires proof of an intent to destroy a group. In the absence of direct evidence of a plan, the court could infer that intent only if it was “the only reasonable inference” from the facts, a high bar to affix responsibility. The facts it accepted are harrowing. In 2017, in what Myanmar’s army called “clearance operations” against the insurgent Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, at least 10,000 Rohingya were killed, 1,834 raped and 392 villages destroyed in northern Rakhine State. Over 7,00,000 fled to Bangladesh. Then Army chief Min Aung Hlaing, now Myanmar’s “civilian” President, called the “Bengali problem” an “unfinished job”. Myanmar argued that it had only been fighting insurgents or at worst, driving the Rohingya out or punishing them. The court said that the army drew no distinction between fighters and civilians, had no plan to move anyone, fired on fleeing people and killed children on a scale that could not be explained as punishment. Seen alongside decades of discrimination, the evidence pointed to an intent to destroy.

The incidents of 2017 were no aberration. The army drove lakhs of Rohingya into Bangladesh in 1978 and 1991-92. The junta stripped the Rohingya of citizenship in 1982 and the state branded them as “foreigners” in Arakan, disenfranchising them in 2015. While the junta’s Bamar-Buddhist vision has oppressed every minority, the Rohingya have been subjected to the most brutality. More than 1.2 million are in Bangladesh, living in dilapidated conditions, made worse due to diminished international aid. The court ordered Myanmar to allow their safe, voluntary and dignified return and to compensate them, but it has no means of enforcing its judgment. Only the UN Security Council can, but it will be subject to vetoes by Myanmar’s backers, China and Russia. On the very day of the verdict, the two joined the U.S. in Shenzhen to declare the “immunities of State officials” of “paramount importance”. Others, India among them, have courted the regime in Naypyitaw regardless, following sham elections that made the junta leader civilian President earlier this year. And Rakhine State, mired in civil war, is now mostly held by the Arakan Army which is accused of atrocities against the Rohingya. Only a truly democratic, federal, plural and peaceful Myanmar can bring the Rohingya home in safety.

While the junta’s Bamar-Buddhist vision has oppressed every minority, the Rohingya have been subjected to the most brutality. More than 1.2 million are in Bangladesh, living in dilapidated conditions, made worse due to diminished international aid. The court ordered Myanmar to allow their safe, voluntary and dignified return and to compensate them, but it has no means of enforcing its judgment. Only the UN Security Council can, but it will be subject to vetoes by Myanmar’s backers, China and Russia. On the very day of the verdict, the two joined the U.S. in Shenzhen to declare the “immunities of State officials” of “paramount importance”. Others, India among them, have courted the regime in Naypyitaw regardless, following sham elections that made the junta leader civilian President earlier this year. And Rakhine State, mired in civil war, is now mostly held by the Arakan Army which is accused of atrocities against the Rohingya. Only a truly democratic, federal, plural and peaceful Myanmar can bring the Rohingya home in safety.
